attribution: Traditionally attributed to Gaudapada, described in the tradition as the teacher of Shankara's teacher Govinda
author: gaudapada
period: Commonly placed around the 6th–7th centuries CE; dating is debated
summary: A verse treatise on the Mandukya Upanishad and the earliest surviving systematic work of Advaita, arguing that nothing has ever truly come into being.
whyRead: The Karika is where Advaita's boldest claims first appear in systematic form: waking is compared to dream, and the doctrine of non-origination (ajativada) holds that the world of multiplicity never really arose. Its vocabulary shows striking overlaps with Mahayana Buddhist thought, a relationship scholars still debate.
questions: Is the waking world more real than a dream?
Can anything truly come into existence?
What remains when all duality is negated?

keyTeachings.title: Commentary on the Mandukya
keyTeachings.text: The first chapter expounds the Mandukya's scheme of Om and the four states, placing the fourth (turiya) beyond all duality.

keyTeachings.title: Waking as like dreaming
keyTeachings.text: The second chapter argues that objects of waking experience share key features with dream objects, and so are not ultimately real.

keyTeachings.title: Non-origination
keyTeachings.text: The central doctrine (ajativada) holds that from the ultimate standpoint nothing is born; there is no dissolution, origination, bondage or seeker of liberation.

keyTeachings.title: The firebrand
keyTeachings.text: The fourth chapter compares apparent multiplicity to the patterns made by a whirling firebrand: movement of consciousness appears as forms that have no separate existence.

structure.label: 4 chapters (prakaranas)
structure.note: Agama, Vaitathya, Advaita and Alatashanti; about 215 verses

passages.about: From the highest standpoint there is no dissolution, origination, bondage or liberation
